title: N-Queens
directAnswer: Place n queens on an n×n board so none attack another, and return every distinct board. The canonical answer is backtracking row by row: each row holds exactly one queen, so try each column, prune any square attacked on its column or either diagonal using three boolean sets (cols, r+c, r−c), choose → recurse to the next row → un-choose. When you place a queen in the last row, build and record the board.

remember.pattern: Row-by-row backtracking with O(1) conflict sets (choose → explore → un-choose)
remember.formula:
def backtrack(row):
    if row == n: results.append(build()); return
    for col in range(n):
        if col in cols or (row+col) in diag or (row-col) in anti: continue   # prune attacks
        place(row, col)            # choose: mark col, row+col, row-col
        backtrack(row + 1)         # explore the next row
        remove(row, col)           # un-choose: unmark all three
rules: Place **one queen per row** and recurse by row — this bakes in the 'no two queens share a row' rule for free.
A square `(row, col)` is safe iff its **column**, its **`row + col`** diagonal, and its **`row − col`** anti-diagonal are all unused — three O(1) set checks.
All cells on a ↘ diagonal share the same `row + col`; all cells on a ↙ anti-diagonal share the same `row − col` — that's why those two sums identify diagonals.
**Choose and un-choose must be symmetric**: marking col, r+c, r−c on the way down means unmarking all three on the way back up.
Record only at `row == n` — a complete, non-attacking placement of all n queens.
Track only **one column per row** (an `int[] queens`), not the full grid — reconstruct the board strings only when you record.
whenToUse: A constraint-satisfaction placement: put k items on a grid with no-conflict rules
Conflicts are checkable incrementally as you place each item
You need all valid configurations (or, for LC 52, the count)
The board/grid is small enough that exponential search with pruning is fine
antiSignals: Only the **count** is needed and n is large → symmetry/known-formula tricks, or it's N-Queens II (still backtracking but no board build)
Conflicts can't be tested until the whole configuration is placed → pruning can't help; rethink the model
It's really a matching/flow problem in disguise → bipartite matching may beat brute search
n is large (≳ 15–20) → the search explodes; the problem likely wants counting heuristics, not enumeration
remember.takeaway: N-Queens is the canonical constraint-satisfaction backtracking problem. The two ideas that make it click — reduce the search by placing one queen per row, and test conflicts in O(1) with the column / `r+c` / `r−c` sets — recur in Sudoku Solver and any 'place items with no-conflict rules' puzzle. Master the symmetric choose/un-choose with diagonal math here and the whole family follows.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you shrink the search space by placing one queen per row, encode the three attack directions as O(1) set lookups (especially the `r+c` / `r−c` diagonal identities), and keep choose/un-choose perfectly symmetric. Bonus: tracking only one column per row instead of a full grid.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Re-scanning the whole board for conflicts (O(n) per check instead of O(1)), getting the diagonal formulas wrong (or only checking one diagonal), forgetting to also check rows (avoided automatically by the one-queen-per-row structure), or asymmetric backtracking that fails to clear all three marks.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the one-queen-per-row reduction, derive WHY `row + col` and `row − col` identify the two diagonals, use boolean sets for O(1) pruning, keep choose/un-choose symmetric, and quote the bound (≈ O(n!) with pruning) plus the int[] queens space optimisation.

problemStatement:
The **n-queens** puzzle is the problem of placing `n` queens on an `n × n` chessboard such that **no two queens attack each other**.

Given an integer `n`, return **all distinct solutions** to the n-queens puzzle. You may return the answer in any order.

Each solution contains a distinct board configuration of the n-queens' placement, where `'Q'` and `'.'` indicate a queen and an empty space, respectively.
understanding: Place n queens so that no two share a row, a column, or a diagonal — the lines along which a chess queen attacks. We must return every distinct full-board configuration as a list of strings. Because every solution has exactly one queen in each row (n queens, n rows, no two in a row), we can search row by row and only ever decide which column the queen in the current row takes.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Does every row contain exactly one queen?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — n queens across n rows with no two in the same row forces exactly one per row. That's the key reduction: we recurse by row and only choose a column each time.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Which lines count as attacks?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Rows, columns, and BOTH diagonals (↘ and ↙). Rows are handled by the one-per-row structure; columns and the two diagonal families need explicit conflict tracking.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do we return boards or just the count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Full boards as lists of strings here. If only the count were required, that's N-Queens II (LC 52) — same search, skip building the board strings.

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can n be?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Up to 9, so the search (≈ n! with diagonal pruning) is small. The hard rating is about the modelling — diagonals and clean backtracking — not raw size.

examples.explanation: The two solutions for a 4×4 board. In the first, queens sit at (0,1),(1,3),(2,0),(3,2) — no two share a column or diagonal.
A single queen on a 1×1 board trivially attacks nothing — one solution.
No way to place 2 non-attacking queens on a 2×2 board — every pair shares a row, column, or diagonal. Same for n = 3.

approaches.name: Row-by-Row Backtracking with Conflict Sets (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The canonical answer. Phrase it as 'one queen per row; for each column check column, r+c and r−c diagonals in O(1); choose/explore/un-choose'.
hints: n queens, n rows, no two in the same row → how many queens must each row hold? What does that let you fix about the search?
Place row by row. For the queen in `row`, try each `col`. You need an O(1) way to ask 'is this square attacked by an earlier queen?' — what three things must be free?

Track used columns in a set, and the two diagonal families: all cells on a ↘ diagonal share `row + col`, all on a ↙ anti-diagonal share `row − col`. Mark all three on choose, clear all three on un-choose.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Placing one queen per row gives at most n choices in row 0, n−1ish in row 1 after pruning, etc., bounded by n! leaves; diagonal/column pruning cuts this dramatically in practice. Each placement check is O(1) via the sets, and building a solution board is O(n²) but happens only at valid leaves. Extra space is the recursion depth (O(n)), the int[] queens (O(n)), and the three sets (O(n)) → O(n) total, excluding output.
approaches.explanation:
Search the board **one row at a time**. Since a valid solution has exactly one queen per row, the only decision at depth `row` is *which column* that row's queen occupies. For each candidate `col` we ask: is `(row, col)` attacked by any queen already placed in rows above? If safe, we **choose** it (mark its column and both diagonals), **explore** by recursing to `row + 1`, then **un-choose** (clear those marks). When `row == n` we've safely placed all n queens, so we materialise the board and record it.

**Why place one queen per row — the search-space reduction.** A naive search over all C(n², n) ways to drop n queens on the board is astronomically large. But 'no two queens share a row' plus 'n queens on n rows' forces exactly one queen per row. Committing to that up front collapses the search to 'pick a column for each row', i.e. essentially a permutation search of size n! — and the row constraint is now satisfied *by construction*, so we never even check it. This reframing from 'choose cells' to 'choose one column per row' is the single most important modelling step.

**Why `row + col` and `row − col` identify the diagonals.** A queen attacks along both diagonals, so we must detect diagonal conflicts in O(1). Observe the geometry: as you walk down-right along a ↘ diagonal, `row` increases by 1 and `col` increases by 1, so `row − col` stays constant — every cell on a given ↘ diagonal shares the same `row − col` value. Symmetrically, walking down-left along a ↙ anti-diagonal, `row` increases while `col` decreases, so `row + col` stays constant. So 'is this square on a diagonal already occupied?' becomes two set-membership tests: `(row − col) in antiDiag` and `(row + col) in diag`. (In array-based variants, offset `row − col` by `n − 1` to keep indices non-negative.) Combined with a `cols` set, three O(1) checks fully decide safety.

**Why choose and un-choose must be perfectly symmetric.** Placing a queen marks three things: its column, its `row + col` diagonal, and its `row − col` anti-diagonal. The backtracking discipline demands that returning from the recursion clears *exactly* those three marks — no more, no less. If you forget to clear even one (say the anti-diagonal), that line stays 'occupied' for every sibling and ancestor branch, and you'll silently miss valid solutions. The cleanest way to guarantee symmetry is to write the three marks and the three un-marks as mirror-image blocks around the recursive call.

**Why store one column per row, not the whole grid.** During the search we only need to know, per row, which column holds the queen — an `int[] queens` of length n captures the entire state and makes un-choosing trivial. We don't need the full n×n character grid until we actually record a solution, at which point we build the strings from `queens`. This keeps the working state O(n) instead of O(n²) and avoids mutating a big grid on every step.
approaches.insight: N-Queens teaches the two universal levers of constraint-satisfaction backtracking: (1) **structure the search so one constraint is satisfied by construction** (one queen per row removes the row check entirely), and (2) **make the remaining conflict tests O(1)** with the right encoding (column and the two diagonal sums). The same playbook — fix one dimension, encode conflicts cheaply, prune early — is exactly how you'd attack Sudoku Solver or any grid-placement puzzle.

dryRun.intro: Place row by row. Safe iff col, row+col (diag), row−col (anti) are all free. Mark on choose, clear on un-choose. Record at row == 4.

steps.action: (1,0) attacked (anti 1−0=1? no; diag 1; col 0 free)… (1,3) safe → mark
(2,0) safe: col 0 free, diag 2, anti 2 free → mark
clear marks, explore the other branch starting (0,2)

code.python:
def solveNQueens(self, n: int) -> list[list[str]]:
    results: list[list[str]] = []
    queens = [-1] * n          # queens[r] = column of the queen in row r
    cols: set[int] = set()
    diag: set[int] = set()     # row + col
    anti_diag: set[int] = set()  # row - col

    def build() -> list[str]:
        return ["." * queens[r] + "Q" + "." * (n - queens[r] - 1) for r in range(n)]

    def backtrack(row: int) -> None:
        if row == n:
            results.append(build())          # all queens placed → record the board
            return
        for col in range(n):
            if col in cols or (row + col) in diag or (row - col) in anti_diag:
                continue                     # square attacked → prune
            queens[row] = col
            cols.add(col)                    # choose
            diag.add(row + col)
            anti_diag.add(row - col)
            backtrack(row + 1)               # explore next row
            cols.remove(col)                 # un-choose
            diag.remove(row + col)
            anti_diag.remove(row - col)

    backtrack(0)
    return results

java.line: boolean[] diag = new boolean[2 * n - 1];       // index by row + col
java.explanation: There are 2n−1 ↘ diagonals; each cell's diagonal is identified by row + col (range 0..2n−2).

java.line: boolean[] antiDiag = new boolean[2 * n - 1];   // index by row - col + (n - 1)
java.explanation: row − col ranges from −(n−1) to n−1; adding n−1 shifts it into 0..2n−2 for array indexing.
Base case: a queen safely placed in every row — a complete solution.

java.line: results.add(build(queens, n));         // all queens placed → record the board
java.explanation: Build the board strings only here, from the compact queens[] state.
The anti-diagonal index, offset by n−1 so it's never negative.

java.explanation: Three O(1) checks decide safety: column, ↘ diagonal, ↙ anti-diagonal. Rows are safe by construction.
CHOOSE: mark all three lines this queen now occupies.
UN-CHOOSE: clear EXACTLY the three marks set above — symmetry is essential.

diagrams.title: Why row+col and row−col name the diagonals
diagrams.caption: Cells on the same ↘ diagonal share a constant row−col; cells on the same ↙ anti-diagonal share a constant row+col. That's what turns a diagonal attack check into an O(1) set lookup.

edgeCases.behavior: row 0 places (0,0); no conflicts possible; row == 1 → record ["Q"]. Returns [["Q"]].
Every column choice in row 0 leaves no safe square in a later row → all branches pruned, returns []. Confirms the prune correctly reports impossibility.

pitfalls: Re-scanning the whole board for conflicts (O(n) per check) instead of O(1) set lookups — turns a fast search slow.
Wrong diagonal formula or checking only one diagonal — produces attacking 'solutions'.
Asymmetric backtracking: marking three lines but failing to clear all three — silently drops valid solutions.
Negative array index for the anti-diagonal — remember the `+ (n − 1)` offset (a set avoids this entirely).

commonMistakes: Checking conflicts by scanning the board in O(n) instead of using O(1) column/diagonal sets.
Getting the diagonal identities wrong — forgetting that ↘ shares row−col and ↙ shares row+col, or checking only one.
Asymmetric choose/un-choose that fails to clear every mark, leaving lines falsely occupied and dropping solutions.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Scanning the board for conflicts
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Walking the column and both diagonals on every candidate is O(n) per check, making the inner work O(n) heavier than needed. Boolean sets answer 'attacked?' in O(1).
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if col in cols or (row + col) in diag or (row - col) in anti_diag:
    continue                              # O(1) checks via sets

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Asymmetric backtracking
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Choosing marks col, row+col and row−col. If un-choose forgets even one (here the anti-diagonal), that line stays occupied for sibling branches and valid boards are silently lost.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
cols.add(col); diag.add(row + col); anti_diag.add(row - col)
backtrack(row + 1)
cols.remove(col); diag.remove(row + col)   # forgot anti_diag!
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
cols.add(col); diag.add(row + col); anti_diag.add(row - col)
backtrack(row + 1)
cols.remove(col); diag.remove(row + col); anti_diag.remove(row - col)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong diagonal identity
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Cells on a ↘ diagonal share row−col, and ↙ anti-diagonals share row+col. Swapping them or only tracking one direction lets diagonally-attacking queens coexist.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
if (row + col) in diag:        # only one diagonal family checked
    continue
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
if (row + col) in diag or (row - col) in anti_diag:   # both directions
    continue

followupVariations.hint: Only the COUNT of solutions is needed → identical row-by-row search, but increment a counter at row == n instead of building and storing boards.

followupVariations.hint: Grid backtracking with a visited marker — choose a cell, explore neighbours, un-choose; the same mark/unmark discipline as the queen conflict sets.

followupVariations.title: Permutations
followupVariations.hint: N-Queens is essentially a constrained permutation (column per row) — the used[]-style tracking and full-length leaf recording are the same core.

patternNote: Canonical Constraint-Satisfaction Backtracking (choose → explore → un-choose) with O(1) conflict sets. Recognise it whenever you place items on a grid under no-conflict rules. The two levers — structure the search so one constraint holds by construction (one queen per row), and encode the rest as O(1) checks (column, row+col, row−col) — also drive Sudoku Solver and Word Search.
